title: Clarifying Requirements & Edge Cases
summary: Turning a deliberately ambiguous prompt into a bounded problem — constraints, edge cases, expected scale — before writing a line of code.

slides.markdown:
"Find the shortest path between two nodes" sounds complete. It isn't. Is the graph weighted? Directed? Can weights be negative? Is it even connected?

Interviewers leave these gaps **on purpose**. The first two to five minutes of a round are a hidden mini-test: can you turn an underspecified prompt into a bounded problem before you commit to code?

Skip this step and you risk building the wrong thing carefully, which scores worse than building the right thing roughly. This topic covers what to ask, what not to bother asking, and when to just state an assumption and move on.

A fully-specified prompt would test one thing: can you translate a spec into code. Real engineering work almost never arrives fully specified — a product ask, a bug report, a one-line Slack message — so interviewers deliberately leave gaps to test whether you **notice** them.

The gap is also a filter for overconfidence. A candidate who starts coding immediately on "find duplicates in a list" without asking whether the list is sorted, whether values repeat more than twice, or whether order must be preserved is demonstrating exactly the habit that causes real bugs: coding the *first* interpretation instead of the *right* one.

The interviewer isn't hiding information to be difficult. They're watching whether you go looking for it.

slides.subTitle: Run it silently on every prompt
slides.markdown:
Five questions cover most of what changes an approach. Run them mentally even when you don't ask all five out loud:

| Check | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Input shape** | Array, string, tree, graph, stream — each implies different tools |
| **Size** | 100 items vs 10⁸ changes whether O(n²) is even viable |
| **Duplicates** | Change correctness of many set/count-based approaches |
| **Ordering** | Sorted input unlocks binary search or two pointers; unsorted doesn't |
| **Nulls / invalid input** | Empty input, negative numbers, malformed entries |

This checklist is a filter, not a script — you don't recite all five for every problem, you scan them and voice the ones whose answer would actually change your code.

slides.sectionTitle: Questions that signal seniority vs questions that stall
slides.markdown:
| Signals seniority | Signals stalling |
|---|---|
| "Can the array be empty, and what should I return?" | "What language should I use?" (usually your choice) |
| "Are we optimizing for time or memory here?" | "Is this problem hard?" |
| "Can weights be negative — that rules out plain Dijkstra" | Re-reading the prompt aloud without asking anything |
| "Should this handle concurrent modification, or is it single-threaded?" | Asking about something already stated in the prompt |

The seniority signal isn't the *number* of questions. It's that each one maps to a concrete fork in your approach. An interviewer can tell within thirty seconds whether a question is diagnostic or a stall tactic.

Given just that prompt, here's a real clarifying sequence and what each answer unlocks:

- **"Is the graph weighted?"** — No → BFS suffices. Yes → need Dijkstra or better.
- **"Can weights be negative?"** — Yes → Dijkstra is wrong; you need Bellman-Ford.
- **"Directed or undirected?"** — Changes how you build the adjacency structure and whether cycles can trap you.
- **"Is the graph guaranteed connected?"** — No → you need to handle "no path exists" as a real return case, not an afterthought.

Four questions, four forks, each changing which algorithm is even correct — not just which is faster. This is what "a question that earns its keep" looks like in practice: each answer eliminates or unlocks a whole approach.

The moment you hear a size constraint, translate it into an allowed complexity — before you've picked an approach. This is a fast mental table worth memorizing:

- **n ≤ ~20** → exponential/backtracking is fine
- **n ≤ ~1,000** → O(n²) or O(n² log n) is fine
- **n ≤ ~10⁵–10⁶** → need O(n log n) or better
- **n ≤ ~10⁸** or a streaming feed → need O(n) or O(1) per element, often single-pass

Stating this out loud ("n up to 10⁵, so O(n²) is too slow, I need n log n") does two things at once: it proves you can reason about complexity, and it prunes the solution space before you've written anything, so you don't waste coding time on an approach that was never going to pass.

The over-correction to "ask clarifying questions" is asking questions reflexively, regardless of whether the answer matters.

Asking "what language should I use?" when you were told at the start, or "can I use extra libraries?" for a problem that obviously expects raw language features, burns time and signals you're following a script rather than actually thinking about *this* problem.

The test before asking anything: **would a different answer change my approach or my code?** If the answer is no matter what, don't ask — state the natural assumption and move on. Interviewers notice the difference between five sharp questions and five reflexive ones just as fast as they notice zero questions.

slides.subTitle: Two failure modes, same prompt
slides.markdown:
| | Under-clarifying | Over-clarifying |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior | Starts coding on the first reading | Spends 8+ minutes on questions before any code |
| Risk | Builds the wrong thing carefully | Runs out of time to actually solve it |
| Reads as | Overconfident, misses real bugs | Anxious, avoiding the hard part |
| Fix | Run the checklist before committing | Ask only questions that fork the approach (§4), then move |

Both failure modes are common, and they're opposite reactions to the same advice — "ask clarifying questions" taken too literally becomes stalling. The two- to five-minute window in §1 is a ceiling, not a suggestion.

slides.sectionTitle: When to just state an assumption
slides.markdown:
Not every ambiguity is worth a question. For low-stakes gaps — case sensitivity in a string match, whether to return `-1` or `null` for "not found" — the efficient move is to **state the assumption out loud and keep going**: "I'll assume this is case-sensitive unless you tell me otherwise."

This does three things a silent assumption doesn't: it surfaces the gap so the interviewer can correct you if you guessed wrong, it doesn't cost the back-and-forth time of a full question, and it's still evidence of noticing the ambiguity in the first place. Reserve actual questions for gaps that would change your algorithm or data structure choice; state-and-proceed for everything else.

Once you've bounded the problem, the next skill is [narrating](narrating-your-approach) the approach you land on, and [recognizing which pattern](pattern-recognition) the constraints point to.

For a much longer worked drill set on question-asking specifically — a full cue sheet and traced examples — see `data-structures-algorithms`'s [clarifying-questions](clarifying-questions) topic; this topic focuses on the checklist and when to skip it, not on drilling variations.
